Singapore Next 50: 4 Mid-Cap Stocks Outperforming the STI in 3Q 2026
article:
Singapore investors had a good third quarter in 2026.
The
SPDR STI ETF
(SGX: ES3), which tracks the
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI), delivered a total return of 11.6% for 3Q2026.
Four mid-cap stocks left that number well behind.
First Resources
(SGX: EB5) topped the list with a 46.4% total return.
Pan-United Corporation
(SGX: P52) followed at 27.9%, while
Golden Agri-Resources
(SGX: E5H), or GAR, and
PC Partner Group
(SGX: PCT) returned 18.5% and 15.9%, respectively.
These figures include
dividends
.
All four companies grew their profits in the first half of 2026 (1H2026).
Look at their cash flows, though, and the picture starts to split.

What might investors see in First Resources?
First Resources is an integrated palm oil producer operating mainly in Indonesia.
For 1H2026, its revenue rose 44.5% year on year (YoY) to US$973.6 million.
Underlying net profit, which excludes biological asset revaluations, grew 42.2% to US$216.2 million.
Part of that growth reflects an easier comparison.
Last year’s first half included only two months from PT Austindo Nusantara Jaya, which the group bought in May 2025.
The cash flow is more convincing.
Free cash flow swung to US$100.6 million from negative US$84.7 million a year ago, and the board lifted the interim dividend by 77.8% to S$0.08 per share.
Investors may also have taken comfort from management’s view that uncertainty around Indonesia’s palm oil export framework has moderated.
There is a catch, however.
Indonesia’s revised export proceeds rules tie up US$115.4 million of the group’s US$229.2 million in cash.

Wilmar vs First Resources: Which Dividend Stock Is Better for Income Investors?

Can Pan-United’s cash flow keep pace with its profit?
Pan-United, Singapore’s largest ready-mix concrete supplier, grew its 1H2026 revenue by 37% YoY to S$549.6 million.
Net profit attributable to shareholders rose 49% to S$30.6 million.
Investors may be looking further ahead.
The Building and Construction Authority (BCA) expects S$47 billion to S$53 billion in construction demand for 2026, and contracts worth S$31 billion had been awarded by June.
Pan-United turned less of its profit into cash.
Free cash flow came in at S$7.4 million, up from S$1 million, while trade and other receivables grew by S$26 million.
The group still holds net cash of S$65.2 million, excluding lease liabilities, and it raised the interim dividend by 50% to S$0.015 per share.
Management is keeping a close eye on
energy costs
and potential supply chain disruptions.
Related articles:
Dividend Surge: 3 SGX Next 50 Stocks Delivering 50%+ Hikes
Beyond STI: 3 Singapore Dividend Stocks Seeing Insider Buying in Q1 2026
Why does GAR deserve a closer look?
GAR is the most complicated of the four.
The Indonesia-centred palm oil company grew revenue 7.3% YoY to US$6.6 billion as the average international crude palm oil (CPO) price rose 8.1% to US$1,178 per tonne.
Profit attributable to shareholders rose 4.4% to US$167.2 million.
GAR booked a US$31.8 million foreign exchange gain, against a US$23.9 million loss a year ago.
That swing of about US$55.7 million is larger than the roughly US$7 million increase in profit, although the foreign exchange figures are before tax.
GAR’s cash flow tells a harder story.
Operating cash flow fell 74% to US$163.8 million as inventories and receivables tied up more cash.
Free cash flow turned negative at -US$58 million, down from a positive US$438.5 million a year ago.
GAR also carries US$3.5 billion in debt, including leases, against US$404.1 million in cash.
GAR did not declare an interim dividend, as it generally reviews its dividend in the second half.
Investors may be betting on management’s view that limited acreage expansion and growing demand will keep CPO prices supported.
Will PC Partner’s margins hold?
PC Partner’s story is about margins, not volume.
Video graphics cards make up 92% of the electronics maker’s revenue.
In 1H2026, revenue rose just 1.5% YoY to HK$6.5 billion, yet profit attributable to owners more than doubled, jumping 117.9% to HK$545.5 million.
Sharply higher graphics card selling prices lifted gross margin to 16.5% from 10.5%.
The cash came through too.
Free cash flow rose to HK$2.5 billion from HK$648.7 million.
The interim dividend of S$0.10 per share, or about HK$0.61, compares with HK$0.25 a year ago.
Its total cost of HK$235.2 million amounts to roughly a tenth of free cash flow.
The next six months look bumpier, as management expects graphics memory costs to keep rising.
New GPU server and AI-related shipments start in the same period, though, and the group remains confident of full-year revenue growth.

title: Korean investors suffer US$1.7 bil losses from leveraged ETFs
article:
(Oct 7): Retail investors are estimated to have lost 2.3 trillion won (US$1.7 billion) from leveraged exchange-traded products tracking South Korea’s two chipmaking giants in just months, according to a lawmaker’s office, in the first revelation of the magnitude of risks from such bets.

Clients of 10 Korean brokerages incurred the losses from single-stock ETFs and notes tied to Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc between May 27 and Aug 14, according to the office of Choi Eun-seok, a lawmaker from the opposition People Power Party.

Since their launch in May, the single-stock products have intensified volatility in Korea’s AI-centric stock market, where leveraged bets have propelled it into one of the world’s top performers before backfiring. The wild swings caused by the risky products have since prompted regulators to cool the fervor among mom-and-pop investors, resulting in a plunge in trading volume.

The data came from the financial watchdog Financial Supervisory Service, which collated information from brokerages including Mirae Asset Securities Co, Kiwoom Securities Co, Samsung Securities Co and NH Investment & Securities Co, Choi’s office said.

Since July, the authorities took measures including a temporary ban on new listings of the leveraged single-stock prodcuts, as well as a higher minimum cash deposit and training requirements for investors. They marked an about-face after regulators introduced the products in May, partly aimed at deterring local investors from piling into similar ETFs listed overseas.

See also: JPMorgan tops global AI banking index with jobs seen to grow

While the leveraged products seek to amplify gains, they can also inflict outsized pain on investors when the tide turns in a market disproportionately exposed to the cycles of the AI industry, where the two Korean chipmakers sit at the centre of its supply chain.

title: Wildfire haze shuts Malaysia schools and looms over Singapore F1
article:
(Oct 7): Worsening air pollution driven by wildfires in Indonesia prompted Malaysia to temporarily shut schools in one of its most populated states, just as a major Formula One race in neighbouring Singapore approaches.

Some 200 schools, kindergartens and nurseries in Johor state’s Bahu Pahat district, about 140km northwest of Singapore, were ordered to close today due to the haze conditions, local media reported. The air quality index in the Malaysian capital of Kuala Lumpur was also in the “very unhealthy” range as of Wednesday morning, ranking the city as the most polluted globally, according to data from IQAir.

Air quality in three of Singapore’s five regions also ranked as unhealthy on Wednesday, days before the city-states’s annual F1 weekend, government data showed.

A spokesperson for Singapore GP Pte Ltd, which organises the race, said it will work closely with relevant agencies “to assess the situation before making any collective decisions regarding the event” should haze cause visibility, public health or operational issues. An F1 spokesperson said conditions are not at any level of concern.

Swaths of Southeast Asia have been clouded in choking smog in recent weeks as Indonesia battles one of its worst wildfire seasons in years. The uncontrolled blazes stem from the long-running use of slash-and-burn agricultural practices, but fire conditions have been exacerbated by an intensifying El Niño that’s parching the landscape.

Environmental group Greenpeace identified more than 20 palm, pulp and sugar companies, including several with links to Malaysia and Singapore, whose land concessions contained sources of smoke from the fires.

See also: Singapore, Malaysia cloaked in haze before key sports events

The number of hotspots last month was the highest since 2015, when a regional haze emergency caused widespread disruptions and diplomatic tensions, according to the Forestry Ministry’s fire-monitoring platform SiPongi.

Last week, organisers of the Kuala Lumpur Standard Chartered Marathon cancelled a kids’ race on health concerns, while pressing on with other race categories, including the full and half marathon distances. Still, top finishers of the full marathon clocked times that were slower than recent years. The marathon was cancelled in 2015.

title: JPMorgan tops global AI banking index with jobs seen to grow
article:
(Oct 6): JPMorgan Chase & Co held its spot as the world’s most advanced bank in artificial intelligence, widening its lead over rivals in an annual ranking that shows AI deployment across the industry is accelerating at a record pace.

Capital One Financial Corp and Royal Bank of Canada retained their second and third places, according to the Evident AI Index that was published on Tuesday. Commonwealth Bank of Australia stayed in fourth position as the only Asia-Pacific lender in the top 10, while UBS Group AG, at sixth place, is the sole European bank in the top leagues. Meanwhile, DBS Group Holdings Ltd, Southeast Asia’s largest bank, ranked 25th, the index showed.

The Evident AI Index seeks to show how global lenders are turning heavy AI spending into results, at a time when banks are facing pressure to justify record tech budgets and concerns brew over whether AI will cost jobs. Lenders that can’t show the technology generates returns risk seeing their AI programs stall, Evident said.

“Roles are changing, and some are not being backfilled, but the banks at the top of our Index are growing, and growing headcount,” Alexandra Mousavizadeh, Evident’s co-founder and co-chief executive officer, said in a statement. “This could be the start of the largest net job creation we have seen in decades.”

Across the 50 banks assessed, AI capabilities improved almost three times faster over the past year than the average across the previous three years, the fastest pace since the index began in 2023.

The leading banks in AI are using productivity gains to grow their business as well as drive efficiencies, Evident said. An example it cites is Wells Fargo & Co training AI agents on 15 years of loan decisions so the process can be automated, with underwriters making the final call.

See also: Taiwan dethrones Korea atop global markets as AI trade widens

Banks are adding AI talent with a focus on enabling people who use the tool, according to Evident, noting that JPMorgan, Commonwealth Bank of Australia and Royal Bank of Canada are the top hirers.

These so-called AI enablement roles, which accelerate deployment of the tech and redesign workflows, grew 21% over the past year across the 50 banks, the fastest of any AI job category. Data engineering roles fell 3%, while other roles like AI development and AI software implementation grew much slower, the Evident report shows.

The index scores the institutions based on their AI talent, research and patent activity, leadership communications and transparency around AI deployment. For JPMorgan, this is the bank’s fifth straight year at the top.

title: Maersk owner seeks investments in Asia startups with new office
article:
(Oct 7): AP Moller Holding A/S, which controls Danish shipping giant AP Moller-Maersk A/S, is opening a new office in Singapore to invest in growth companies in Asia.

The firm, funded entirely by the billionaire Maersk family with no external investors, will open the office — its first outside of Denmark — this week. It has more than US$50 billion ($64 billion) of net assets.

“Asia is at the forefront of global innovation,” said Chetan Mehta, head of growth investing at the firm, who is going to lead the Asia office. “As many of these world-leading late-stage startups are looking to expand, that gives us an opportunity to provide them the long-term funding.”

The Danish investment company is looking to take minority stakes, typically €20 million (US$22.4 million or $28.7 million) to €80 million, from Series C startups to IPO-stage firms and beyond, Mehta said in an interview.

The startups will mostly be in the applied technology sector, such as AI supply chains, fintech, healthcare and robotics. The firm will be looking at firms across China, India, Southeast Asia, Australia and New Zealand, he added.

In Europe, AP Moller Holding is an existing investor in French online healthcare platform Doctolib, Finnish satellite maker Iceye and UK fintech giant Revolut. It led the €80 million equity funding round of UK neo-bank Zopa in 2024, and is the largest shareholder of Danske Bank A/S.

See also: Rhine drops below shipping threshold as freight costs rise

“We are investing our own money without a hard exit deadline nor fund life, so we can be really flexible and support the startups along their growth journey,” Mehta said.

title: Taiwan dethrones Korea atop global markets as AI trade widens
article:
(Oct 7): As equity investors enter the final stretch of a pivotal year that’s propelled South Korea and Taiwan to the forefront of the global AI trade, the latter is emerging as the stronger bet.

The Taiex Index beat the Kospi by about 23 percentage points last quarter, the widest margin since the turn of the century. Earnings upgrades also outpaced those for its Korean peer for the first time since March 2025. About 40% of the fund managers surveyed by Bank of America Corp. last month said they were overweight Taiwan, versus 25% for Korea.

Driving the optimism are Taiwan’s deeper linkages across the AI supply chain and a more upbeat earnings outlook.

“The distinction for us is not simply the amount of AI exposure, but the nature of the earnings supporting it,” said Vikas Pershad, a portfolio manager at M&G Investments in Singapore. “Taiwan offers a broader and deeper opportunity set. Its earnings come from volume and that makes its earnings upgrades broader and stickier. Korea’s earnings, in the near-term, are coming from price.”

Taiwan offers investors exposure across chip design and manufacturing, packaging, networking, and servers, meaning it has more ways to benefit as AI spending broadens. Korea’s market leadership, meanwhile, remains heavily concentrated in chipmakers Samsung Electronics Co. and SK Hynix Inc., leaving it more vulnerable as doubts emerge over how much longer the current memory upcycle can run.

See also: Citi takes top spot in global IPO underwriting through September

The Taiex and Kospi have traded places at the top of the global leaderboard this year, even as the latter has dominated headlines for its more eye-catching moves. Up 72% in 2026, Taiwan’s benchmark is currently the top performer among more than 90 equity indexes tracked by Bloomberg. The Kospi is ranked second, with gains of about 65%.

Taiwan’s lead comes as shares of Samsung and SK Hynix plunged between 19% and 33% in the three months ended September. That followed a six-quarter winning streak as surging memory-chip prices drove blockbuster earnings and fueled rapid profit upgrades from analysts.

Societe Generale SA is “keeping a preference for Taiwan over Korean equities, given the diverging earnings growth trajectories,” strategists including Rajat Agarwal wrote in note. Memory “price appreciation is expected to slow over coming quarters, before normalization in 2028” as Chinese competition rises, while Korea’s July deleveraging has broadened into a wider retreat from the market, they wrote.

The counter view is AI-related demand will exacerbate the ongoing semiconductor supply shortage, keeping prices for high-bandwidth memory chips supported. Peter Lee, a managing director at Citigroup Inc who jointly oversees its global tech and communication research, said last week that investors should start buying shares of firms like Samsung and SK Hynix as the market is underestimating how much HBM chips will be needed in 2027.

In terms of valuations, the Taiex is trading at about 18 times its one-year forward estimated earnings. The Kospi trades at around 5.5 times, reflecting concern that the memory cycle may be approaching a peak, and in part the longstanding “Korea discount” that has kept the market cheap relative to global peers.

Still, when asked which market would benefit the most from the next phase of the AI cycle, 35% of the respondents in the BofA survey chose Taiwan. Just 5% picked Korea.

Shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. rose 2.9% in the three months to September, capping a sixth straight quarterly advance.

But Taiex is delivering broader gains than its other tech-heavy peers, reflecting a wider range of investment opportunities. About 10% of the gauge’s stocks have at least doubled this year, compared with 4.1% for the Kospi and 5.7% for Japan’s Nikkei 225.

“The next leg of upside for Taiwan stocks is likely to depend less on broad AI enthusiasm and more on local tech companies that remain exposed to genuine bottlenecks in the AI value chain,” said Gary Tan, portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments.

title: From insight to influence, CPA Australia shapes the finance leaders of tomorrow
article:
Much has been said about how the adoption of AI and technology is enhancing efficiency and increasing productivity.

This is confirmed by CPA Australia’s own survey which found that investment in technology consistently strengthens business performance.

According to the CPA Australia Business Technology Report 2026, organisations that harness technology are more likely to be more profitable and operationally efficient, with artificial intelligence (AI) helping to increase productivity and improve the experience of employees.

The report highlights accounting and finance teams are most likely to use AI in data analytics, insights, communications, administrative process automation, data quality and workplace learning, highlights the report.

“The volume and speed of data have increased, and a finance leader can no longer personally process every document, transaction or market update using traditional methods,” notes Andy Lee, a CPA Australia member and finance director at STTGDC.

Lee says finance leaders have evolved from being custodians of historical financial data to architects of forward-looking decisions. In the fast-moving data centre sector where Lee operates, this means decisions must be made quickly using large volumes of data from multiple sources.

“How do we make decision at speed? The data centre sector changes rapidly,” says Lee. “It's important to have empowered finance leaders that can use the data available to guide them quickly and accurately.”

Due to technology augmenting capabilities, Lee adds that stakeholders increasingly value finance leaders’ ability to interpret data, anticipate risks, challenge assumptions and communicate what should happen next.

“When information can be searched, analysed and visualised in a matter of minutes, finance teams can devote more attention to interpreting insights, anticipating risks and supporting better business decisions,” Lee says.

Echoing similar sentiments, Dominic Ong FCPA (Aust.), CFO of wealth platform Endowus, says that expectations of response speed from finance leaders have changed, with boards and investors expecting answers in days rather than weeks.

“There's more automation, and more is now possible than ever before. This means businesses expect finance leaders to expand their scope beyond the traditional accounting function,” suggests Ong.

Ong says that the biggest shift he has observed is finance leaders becoming business leaders, particularly in growth start-ups environments.

“Certainly, with the CFOs I meet, more of them seem to hold formal business responsibilities along with their finance roles, says Ong.

In addition, changing stakeholder expectations and an increasingly complex business environment are both driving this evolution of finance leaders into business leaders.

“Interest-rate volatility, geopolitical risk, regulation, sustainability requirements and rapid technological development are interconnected, and finance teams have to bring those issues together into a coherent view,” says Lee, adding that finance helps stakeholders to make decisions.

At STTGDC, Lee’s responsibilities span corporate treasury activities to support the company’s growth, encompassing funding and capital management, liquidity oversight, debt and risk management, equity funding, management and board reporting and providing support to subsidiaries across multiple markets.

He says that he enjoys his work as corporate treasury sits at the intersection of finance, strategy, risk and the capital markets.

“We are not only reporting what has happened, but also helping the organisation decide what it can fund, when it should fund it and how risk should be allocated,” says Lee.

Meanwhile, Ong’s dual mandate at Endowus includes undertaking CFO responsibilities and spearheading business development. Joining a start-up, Ong had to build the finance and business development functions from scratch.

From his perspective, the business environment has become less forgiving. “After the financial crisis and the pandemic, tolerance for surprises fell close to zero, which puts finance in the room to inform decisions rather than only reporting on them.”.

He adds that the drive to increasing automation in the professions is also due to talent scarcity. “Fewer people are entering the profession in this region than demand requires, so if you cannot hire through growth, you find a way to automate it.”

For context, from 2018 to 2024, the first-year intake of accountancy students at Singapore’s autonomous universities declined significantly. For instance, Nanyang Technological University’s accountancy intake dropped by more than 40% from 541 in 2018 to 314 in 2024.

Overall, accountancy cohort sizes in Singapore's autonomous universities have dropped by more than 10% since 2018, according to data from the Singapore Yearbook of Manpower Statistics 2024.

To tackle the accounting talent shortage, the Singapore's Ministry of Finance (MOF) and the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA) established the Accounting Workforce Review Committee (AWRC) in 2022 to enhance the attractiveness of the accountancy profession. In 2024, the AWRC shared a report which put forth recommendations to build a quality and sustainable talent pipeline for the accountancy profession.

Singapore’s estimated accountancy workforce was estimated to be 120,000 in 2024, up from the 100,000 in 2022. With Singapore growing as a major wealth and finance hub, demand for accounting and finance professionals is expected to grow.

AI as a co-pilot, not an autopilot

Between 2022 and 2026, businesses steadily increased their adoption of digital technologies, according to CPA Australia’s Business Technology Report 2026, with AI seeing the most dramatic growth, rising from moderate usage levels to near-universal adoption in 2025 and 2026.

From his personal experience, Lee says that AI has reduced the time spent searching, extracting, comparing information while accelerating the preparation of financing analyses, treasury reports and management materials. Its more strategic role is to help finance professionals identify patterns, surface exceptions and consider alternative scenarios.

As his AI skills and confidence in the technology grew, Lee began using AI to support decision-making by providing quicker access to relevant data, highlighting key considerations, and enabling more informed discussions with stakeholders.

“Rather than replacing professional judgement, AI became a tool that helped accelerate analysis, improve productivity, and free up more time to focus on strategic issues to contribute to the business,” says Lee.

“I see AI as a co-pilot for finance, not an autopilot,” he adds.

Meanwhile for Ong, he shares that AI has helped him and his team win back time from time-consuming manual work. Examples include expediting expense claims and requests from other teams with AI.

Ong is also clear where AI is still unable to replace a human such as recording and approving transactions. He points out that AI may give his team time back, but it doesn't do the accounting.

He adds, “We clearly attest in our audit reports that they are not prepared by AI. The books and accounting are entirely the work of our team.”

From his perspective of working for a wealth platform, Ong shares some caution about the use of AI and how it could erode trust if not used correctly.

“We're in a business where trust accrues slowly but is lost very quickly. That's our business model,” he says.

“A tool that makes you faster is valuable, but a tool that makes you faster and occasionally confidently wrong, with nobody checking, costs more than it saves. We have to tread very carefully, especially in the finance function.”

Another risk he sees creeping across the broader workforce is the de-skilling of junior staff resulting from AI use.

“Junior staff used to do a lot of routine work, and that's where you learn the job and develop your instinct, but now, your juniors come in and they don't develop that instinct,” shares Ong.

“That’s going to be a challenge as they grow through the ranks over the next decade, because you’ll have a cohort of people who have not gone through doing the grunt work and learned from it.”

Ong adds that Endowus is deliberately keeping some of the routine work to train junior staff.

The new economic and business landscape requires accounting and finance leaders to develop new skills that go beyond technical accountancy expertise and AI skills.

For Lee, professional scepticism and judgment are needed to harness AI effectively, especially in identifying mistakes made by AI. He believes that AI should operate within a controlled finance framework.

“It can propose an analysis, but a finance professional remains accountable for the numbers, assumptions, interpretation and decision,” says Lee.

He shares that the CPA qualification offers finance leaders both a technical foundation and an ethical compass, both of importance in an AI-enabled world.

“A CPA has to use their judgement to assess if the information from AI is complete, the assumptions are reasonable and the proposed action is responsible.”

He adds that his CPA journey has made him a more complete finance professional, elevating him into a business leader.

“Becoming a CPA has complemented my background in banking, treasury and capital markets, while strengthening my ability to connect financing decisions with accounting, governance and long-term business value.”

Similarly, Ong believes that being a CPA has helped develop his professional scepticism muscle. He adds that commercial judgement, communication and strategic thinking are important skills for financial and business leaders.

“What matters is what you do in the room when decisions are made, where you are often the only person who can see the whole picture and tie the decision back to what it does financially,” Ong elaborates.

“Those are really the key skills that help you to then connect the dots between the decisions we make and the financials.”

Ong also believes that the CPA qualification is highly recognised in the world of finance.

“It signals a professional standard and a code of ethics behind your judgement. The designation is also recognised across markets, so your career is not tied to a single location,” he says.

Being both finance and business leaders, Lee and Ong are responsible for leading outcomes for their respective organisations. To be effective in their roles, they are active in attending continuous professional development (CPD) and networking events organised by CPA Australia, such as the CPA Congress, among others.

As the role of a finance professional continues to expand beyond reporting and analysis, CPA Congress 2026 focuses on how finance leaders can lead better outcomes for your business.

This year’s programme supports finance leaders to move from insight to influence by building the systems, metrics and confidence that are required to shape results.

One of the overseas events will be held on Nov 5 in Kuala Lumpur. Guest speakers include Professor Kishore Mahbubani, distinguished fellow of the Asia Research Institute and former president of the UN Security Council and UOB Malaysia CEO Datuk Ng Wei Wei.

You may attend the event in person or join virtual live.

title: Malaysian PM Anwar set to boost budget spending as election speculation grows
article:
(Oct 7): Malaysian Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim is expected to tackle rising living costs in potentially his government’s last budget before he calls national elections.

Anwar, who is also the finance minister, is likely to prioritise cash handouts to middle-income groups when he presents the 2027 spending plan to parliament on Friday. He’ll also likely provide more support for the semiconductor and renewable-energy sectors, and aim to boost existing revenue streams instead of unveiling new taxes, economists said.

The 79-year-old premier, whose Pakatan Harapan coalition has suffered setbacks in a succession of state elections, is trying to court voters and is said to be considering calling nationwide polls in the second half of next year, ahead of the February 2028 deadline.

That “raises the stakes for every measure inside the 2027 budget,” Kenanga Investment Bank Bhd economists said in a report that noted a pledge to protect people from the global energy crisis while laying the foundations for a higher-value economy. “The main aim is to ease cost-of-living pressure on households.”

On Aug 30, Anwar restored subsidized fuel quotas in a move that could benefit 16 million people even as it adds to deficit pressures, and eased a burdensome invoicing regulation for small and medium enterprises. He has also signaled a possible hike in the private sector’s monthly minimum wage from RM1,700 (US$416 or $532), with the economy minister identifying higher wages as a key priority.

“Rising political noise ahead of the Budget 2027 announcement, taken together with persistent external volatility and elevated oil prices, suggests that fiscal consolidation may prove challenging,” Lavanya Venkateswaran, economist at Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp said in a report.

See also: Oil, AI demand give ringgit room to rally, strategists say

Spending on subsidies and social assistance could push the government’s 2026 fiscal deficit to 3.6% of gross domestic product, compared with its 3.5% target, she said.

While state spending on fuel subsidies could climb to RM40 billion in 2026, more than double the RM15 billion allocated in this year’s budget, tax revenue should also be strong. That’s thanks to an economy that expanded a faster-than-expected 6% in the second quarter from a year earlier.

For 2027, the government will likely project a narrower fiscal deficit of 3.4% of GDP, according to a Bloomberg survey of economists.

See also: Penang E&E players face capacity crunch amid influx of orders

“We expect a mildly expansionary yet fiscally measured budget, balancing growth priorities with fiscal discipline,” UOB Kay Hian economists said in a report. It may include “increased cash handouts and increased tax reliefs for the middle-income group.”

Malaysia’s tech-exporting economy has benefited from the artificial intelligence boom, and UOB Kay Hian says the sector could get further support through tax incentives, grants, preferential financing as well as measures to promote research and talent development. It also forecasts green incentives to help Malaysia reach net zero carbon emissions by 2050.

The central bank expects the economy to expand about 5% this year, at the upper end of its 4%-5% forecast range. Bank Negara Malaysia expects inflation to remain manageable and within its 1.5%-2.5% outlook this year, with consumer prices rising 1.9% in August from a year ago.

Economists surveyed by Bloomberg see next year’s GDP growth at 4.8%, with headline inflation at 2.1% in 2027.

Even as growth remains resilient, Anwar has acknowledged that strong economic performance has yet to translate into an improved sense of economic well-being for many Malaysians. It’s unclear if populist measures will help revive his government’s prospects.

The nation has limited room for additional spending as it seeks to narrow its budget deficit, with fiscal discipline important for maintaining investor confidence, according to Azizul Amiludin, a senior fellow at the Malaysian Institute of Economic Research.

“Many of the challenges associated with the cost of living are structural in nature, and policy interventions typically take time to translate into tangible outcomes,” Azizul said. “Addressing these challenges therefore requires sustained and longer-term policy measures rather than one-off budgetary support.”
